claim: The mitochondrial genomes of apicomplexans comprise merely three protein-coding genes.
source: The mitochondrial genomes of apicomplexans comprise merely three protein-coding genes, alongside a set of thirty to forty genes encoding small RNAs (sRNAs), many of which exhibit homologies to rRNA from E. coli.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes.

claim: Apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes contain thirty to forty genes encoding small RNAs (sRNAs).
source: The mitochondrial genomes of apicomplexans comprise merely three protein-coding genes, alongside a set of thirty to forty genes encoding small RNAs (sRNAs), many of which exhibit homologies to rRNA from E. coli.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the number of sRNA genes.

claim: Many apicomplexan mitochondrial sRNAs exhibit homologies to rRNA from E. coli.
source: The mitochondrial genomes of apicomplexans comprise merely three protein-coding genes, alongside a set of thirty to forty genes encoding small RNAs (sRNAs), many of which exhibit homologies to rRNA from E. coli.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about sequence homology.

claim: Direct evidence for active ribosomes within apicomplexan mitochondria is still lacking.
source: The expression status and integration of these short RNAs into ribosomes remains unclear and direct evidence for active ribosomes within apicomplexan mitochondria is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in current knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The T. gondii mitochondrial genome comprises 21 sequence blocks that undergo recombination among themselves.
source: It has been established previously that the T. gondii genome comprises 21 sequence blocks that undergo recombination among themselves but that their order is not entirely random.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as previously established knowledge.

claim: The order of T. gondii mitochondrial sequence blocks is not entirely random.
source: It has been established previously that the T. gondii genome comprises 21 sequence blocks that undergo recombination among themselves but that their order is not entirely random.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as previously established knowledge.

claim: Many small RNAs originated from the junction sites between protein-coding blocks and rRNA sequence blocks.
source: Employing this refined genome for sRNA mapping, we find that many small RNAs originated from the junction sites between protein-coding blocks and rRNA sequence blocks.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the study's data.

claim: Block border sRNAs were incorporated into polysomes together with canonical rRNA fragments and mRNAs.
source: Surprisingly, such block border sRNAs were incorporated into polysomes together with canonical rRNA fragments and mRNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the study's data.

claim: Apicomplexan ribosomes are active within polysomes.
source: In conclusion, apicomplexan ribosomes are active within polysomes and are indeed assembled through the integration of sRNAs, including previously undetected sRNAs with merged mRNA-rRNA sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Apicomplexan ribosomes are assembled through the integration of sRNAs.
source: In conclusion, apicomplexan ribosomes are active within polysomes and are indeed assembled through the integration of sRNAs, including previously undetected sRNAs with merged mRNA-rRNA sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: T. gondii's block-based genome organization enables the dual utilization of mitochondrial sequences as both messenger RNAs and ribosomal RNAs.
source: Our findings lead to the hypothesis that T. gondii's block-based genome organization enables the dual utilization of mitochondrial sequences as both messenger RNAs and ribosomal RNAs, potentially establishing a link between the regulation of rRNA and mRNA expression.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the study's findings.

claim: Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii.
source: Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, one of the most widespread human parasites, with a seroprevalence of more than one-quarter of humans worldwide (Molan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: T. gondii has a seroprevalence of more than one-quarter of humans worldwide.
source: Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, one of the most widespread human parasites, with a seroprevalence of more than one-quarter of humans worldwide (Molan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: T. gondii remains an ideal model system for studying the molecular biology of Apicomplexa.
source: For many experimental questions, T. gondii remains an ideal model system for studying the molecular biology of Apicomplexa (Szabo and Finney, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: Apicomplexan cells possess a single mitochondrion that is respirationally active and essential for parasite survival.
source: Apicomplexan cells possess a single mitochondrion that is respirationally active and essential for parasite survival (MacRae et al., 2012; Melo et al., 2000; Seeber et al., 1998; Vercesi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with multiple citations to support it.

claim: All mitochondrial proteins except three are nuclear-encoded in apicomplexans.
source: With only three exceptions, all mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and these nuclear genes contribute strongly to P. berghei and T. gondii cell fitness (Bushell et al., 2017; Sidik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins contribute strongly to P. berghei and T. gondii cell fitness.
source: With only three exceptions, all mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and these nuclear genes contribute strongly to P. berghei and T. gondii cell fitness (Bushell et al., 2017; Sidik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes range in length from 6 to 11 kb.
source: These sequences showcase the extreme reductive evolution in apicomplexan mitochondria, setting records for the smallest mitochondrial genomes known to date, ranging in length from 6 to 11 kb (Hikosaka et al., 2013; Oborník and Lukeš, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Some apicomplexan species have a linear, monomeric mitochondrial genome (Babesia spp.).
source: Mitochondrial genome organization is evolutionarily very variable, with some species having a linear, monomeric genome (Babesia spp.), while others have concatenated arrays of genomes (Hikosaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: The T. gondii mitochondrial genome is composed of 21 repetitive sequence blocks that are organized on multiple DNA molecules of varying lengths and non-random combinations.
source: The T. gondii mitochondrial genome is composed of 21 repetitive sequence blocks that are organized on multiple DNA molecules of varying lengths and non-random combinations (Berná et al., 2021a; Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Apicomplexan mitogenomes code only for three proteins (COB, COX1, COXIII).
source: Apicomplexan mitogenomes code only for three proteins (COB, COX1, COXIII) and have highly fragmented genes for rRNAs (Feagin et al., 2012; Seeber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: In P. falciparum, 34 genes for rRNA fragments are scattered across the mitochondrial DNA on both strands of the genome.
source: For example, in P. falciparum, 34 genes for rRNA fragments are scattered across the mitochondrial DNA on both strands of the genome without any linear representation of the full-length large or small subunit rRNA (Feagin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: A nuclear-encoded RNA polymerase targeted to mitochondria has been shown to be essential in the blood stages of Plasmodium spp.
source: In fact, a nuclear-encoded RNA polymerase targeted to mitochondria has been shown to be essential in the blood stages of Plasmodium spp. (Ke et al., 2012; Suplick et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Two mitochondrially localized RNA binding proteins from the RAP family are essential for the survival of P. falciparum.
source: Two mitochondrially localized RNA binding proteins from the RAP (RNA-binding domain abundant in apicomplexans) family are also essential for the survival of P. falciparum, although their role in RNA metabolism has not yet been determined (Hollin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: Depletion of nuclear-encoded mitoribosomal proteins of T. gondii led to defects in the assembly of ETC complexes and in parasite proliferation.
source: In addition, the depletion of nuclear-encoded mitoribosomal proteins of T. gondii (Lacombe et al., 2019; Shikha et al., 2022) and P. falciparum (Ke et al., 2018) led to defects in the assembly of ETC complexes and in parasite proliferation, suggesting that mitochondrial translation is important for parasite survival.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Resistance to the antimalarial drug atovaquone in P. falciparum and T. gondii has been linked to mutations in the cob (cytB) gene of mitochondria.
source: Resistance to the antimalarial drug atovaquone in P. falciparum and T. gondii has been linked to mutations in the cob (cytB) gene of mitochondria (McFadden et al., 2000; Srivastava et al., 1999; Syafruddin et al., 1999), further supporting the idea of active, essential translation in apicomplexan mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Genome-length, polycistronic transcripts are produced in Plasmodium that encompass all three open reading frames.
source: Genome-length, polycistronic transcripts are produced in Plasmodium that encompass all three open reading frames (Ji et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: The existence of full-length mRNAs was confirmed by cDNA amplifications and long-read sequencing of mRNAs in both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
source: The existence of full-length mRNAs was further confirmed by cDNA amplifications (Namasivayam et al., 2021) and long-read sequencing of mRNAs in both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma (Lee et al., 2021; Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: There is no evidence of dedicated transcription initiation for individual protein-coding genes in apicomplexan mitochondria.
source: There is no evidence of dedicated transcription initiation for individual protein-coding genes, and it is assumed that mRNAs are processed from the polycistronic precursor (Feagin et al., 2012; Hillebrand et al., 2018; Rehkopf et al., 2000; Suplick et al., 1990), but the mechanism of processing and the required machinery are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: The production of rRNA fragments is achieved post-transcriptionally by processing long precursor RNAs.
source: Similarly, the production of rRNA fragments is achieved post-transcriptionally by processing long precursor RNAs (Ji et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: A catalog of small RNAs, mostly rRNA fragments, was described for P. falciparum based on small RNA sequencing.
source: A catalog of small RNAs, mostly rRNA fragments, was described for P. falciparum based on small RNA sequencing (Hillebrand et al., 2018), but in other apicomplexans, including T. gondii, our understanding of rRNA species is limited, and mostly based on predictions through sequence comparisons with Plasmodium (Feagin et al., 2012; Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: The T. gondii nuclear genome contains many insertions of mitochondrial DNA sequences.
source: The T. gondii nuclear genome contains many insertions of mitochondrial DNA sequences (Gjerde, 2013; Namasivayam et al., 2023; Ossorio et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Digitonin selectively permeabilizes sterol-rich membranes, leaving mitochondria and other organelles intact.
source: We incubated cells with the detergent digitonin, which selectively permeabilizes sterol-rich membranes, leaving mitochondria and other organelles intact.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on known properties of digitonin.

claim: Mitochondrial GFP remained in the pellet fraction with only a minor signal in the supernatant, indicating that the mitochondria remained largely intact.
source: We observed that mitochondrial GFP remained in the pellet fraction (P in Figure 1B) with only a minor signal in the supernatant, indicating that the mitochondria remained largely intact.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cytosolic HSP70 largely remained in the supernatant after digitonin and benzonase treatment, indicating that the method successfully reduced cytoplasmic proteins.
source: In contrast, cytosolic HSP70 largely remained in the supernatant after digitonin and benzonase treatment, indicating that the method successfully reduced cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cytosolic 18 S and 26 S rRNA were almost completely degraded, indicating the high efficacy of the benzonase treatment.
source: We also found that cytosolic 18 S and 26 S rRNA were almost completely degraded, indicating the high efficacy of the benzonase treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The enhanced protocol for organellar enrichment effectively depletes cytosolic protein and RNA components and enriches mitochondrial macromolecules.
source: In summary, our enhanced protocol for organellar enrichment effectively depletes cytosolic protein and RNA components and enriches mitochondrial macromolecules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results shown in Figure 1.

claim: SSUD and LSUF were protected from benzonase degradation.
source: In contrast, we observed clear bands for both SSUD and LSUF, indicating their protection from benzonase degradation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After filtering against the nuclear genome, 86,761 reads had similarities to the published mitochondrial genome sequence.
source: After filtering against the nuclear genome, we found 86,761 reads that had similarities to the published mitochondrial genome sequence (Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The mitochondrial reads account for 9.2% of the total sequences attributed to the nucleus and mitochondria.
source: This corresponds to 78.5 Mbp, which accounts for 9.2% of the total sequences that we attribute to the nucleus and mitochondria (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: This is a 42-fold increase in the sequencing depth of the T. gondii mitochondrial genome compared to previous attempts.
source: This is a 42-fold increase in the sequencing depth of the T. gondii mitochondrial genome compared to previous attempts (Supplementary file 1), which can be attributed to the effectiveness of the purification process.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's results with previous studies.

claim: The length of mitochondrial reads ranged from 87 nt to 17,424 nt.
source: The length of mitochondrial reads ranged from 87 nt to 17,424 nt (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The GC content of mitochondrial reads, on average 36.4%, supports their mitochondrial origin.
source: The GC content of these reads, on average 36.4%, further supports their mitochondrial origin (Berná et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis with a citation for comparison.

claim: The study confirmed the previously described 21 sequence blocks, designated by letters from A-V.
source: We annotated the reads using published sequence block information (Namasivayam et al., 2021) and confirmed the previously described 21 sequence blocks, designated by letters from A-V (Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: No additional blocks were found, suggesting that the T. gondii mitochondrial genome is fully covered.
source: We searched the sequencing data for repeated sequence elements but found no additional blocks, suggesting that the T. gondii mitochondrial genome is fully covered.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The actual block order was reshuffled by recombination, indicating the rapidity of mitogenome evolution in T. gondii.
source: This suggests that while the block content is identical between the different sequencing results, the actual block order was reshuffled by recombination, indicating the rapidity of mitogenome evolution in T. gondii, thus corroborating at a deeper sequencing coverage conclusions so far gained from a more limited read set (Berná et al., 2021a; Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the current study's results with previous studies.

claim: The most frequent block, J, occurred 45,849 times and the least frequent, C, occurred 3138 times.
source: We observed that the rate of occurrence of blocks varies dramatically in our dataset, with the most frequent block, J, occurring 45,849 times and the least frequent, C, occurring 3138 times (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only a small fraction of all possible block combinations are prevalent within the genome.
source: After counting block combinations, we found that only a small fraction of all possible block combinations are prevalent within the genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4), confirming block combinations observed previously (Namasivayam et al., 2021) and adding combination frequencies based on higher read numbers.
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The most frequent block combination is J-B, which occurs 19,622 times.
source: For example, the most frequent block combination is J-B, which occurs 19,622 times in our reads.
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Fourteen blocks are always found with the same preceding and following block.
source: Fourteen blocks (R, N, M, F, L, U, I, C, K, D, H, E, T) are always found with the same preceding and following block.
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The direction of the blocks in these combinations is fixed.
source: The direction of the blocks in these combinations is fixed (for example, the 3'-end of the L block is always fused to the 5'-end of the J block, never to the 3'-end of the J-block).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Not all block combinations are realized in the T. gondii mitochondrial genome.
source: This indicates that the genome's flexibility is limited and that not all block combinations are realized (see also Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The three 5'-ends of protein-coding genes are always flanked by blocks also encoding a protein.
source: For example, when considering the positioning of the three protein-coding genes within this map, it is conspicuous that their three 5'-ends are always flanked by blocks also encoding a protein (Figure 2B), although it is unclear whether this is of functional relevance.
evidence: This is an observation from the DNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full-length coding regions had been found previously on nanopore reads in T. gondii.
source: Full-length coding regions had been found previously on nanopore reads in T. gondii (Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: A large number of full representations of cob, coxI, and coxIII were identified in the dataset (cob: 1612; coxI: 1404; coxIII: 1487).
source: In our improved representation of the mitogenome, we identified a large number of full representations of cob, coxI, and coxIII in our dataset (cob: 1612; coxI: 1404; coxIII: 1487).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Of all reads long enough to carry one of the ORFs, 5.1% contain full-length coxIII, 8.6% contain full-length cob, and 11.1% full-length cox1.
source: Thus, of all reads long enough to carry one of the following ORFs, 5.1% contain full-length coxIII, 8.6% contain full-length cob, and 11.1% full-length cox1, respectively (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Block S, as part of the coxI coding region, was followed in 80% of its occurrences by the rRNA block R and only in 20% by the next coding block C.
source: For example, block S, as part of the coxI coding region, was followed in 80% of its occurrences by the rRNA block R and only in 20% by the next coding block C (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Block B, as part of the coxIII reading frame, was followed in 66% of all cases by the rRNA block U and less frequently by the terminal block of coxIII, which is block M.
source: Similarly, block B, as part of the coxIII reading frame, was followed in 66% of all cases by the rRNA block U and less frequently by the terminal block of coxIII, which is block M.
evidence: This is a result from the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The 5'-termini of mitochondrial small RNAs are clearly defined.
source: The results of our mapping study show that the 5'-termini of mitochondrial small RNAs are clearly defined, making it easy to identify their transcript ends (as shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 3'-ends of many transcripts were more variable.
source: In agreement with findings from previous studies on small RNAs from P. falciparum (Hillebrand et al., 2018), we found that the 3'-ends of many transcripts were more variable (as seen in the example of RNA17 in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A total of 34 small RNAs accumulate in T. gondii mitochondria.
source: We identified a total of 34 small RNAs that accumulate in T. gondii mitochondria (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Among the 34 small RNAs, 11 correspond to previously predicted rRNA fragments.
source: Among these, 11 correspond to previously predicted rRNA fragments (Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis compared with previous predictions.

claim: SSUF was reassigned to the opposite strand.
source: This included a reassignment of SSUF to the opposite strand and also affected the four rRNA fragments LSUF, LSUG, LSUD, and LSUE, which had been predicted as separate transcripts of the large subunit (LSU) of the ribosome (Namasivayam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis that differs from previous predictions.

claim: There is an accumulation of transcripts containing LSUF and LSUG regions and LSUD and LSUE regions, respectively.
source: Our sequencing results suggest that there is an accumulation of transcripts containing LSUF and LSUG regions and LSUD and LSUE regions, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Both of these transcripts were verified via northern blotting.
source: Both of these transcripts were verified via northern blotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the northern blotting experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The longer transcripts were found to be much more abundant than smaller transcripts.
source: The longer transcripts were found to be much more abundant than smaller transcripts that were also detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the longer transcripts represent the functional rRNA fragments in T. gondii mitochondria.
evidence: This is a result from the northern blotting experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Out of the 34 small RNA fragments identified, 23 have not been described previously for T. gondii.
source: Out of the 34 small RNA fragments identified, 23 have not been described previously for T. gondii (see Supplementary file 7 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: 17 of the 23 newly identified sRNAs are homologs of sRNA fragments in the apicomplexans P. falciparum and E. leuckarti.
source: 17 of the 23 are homologs of sRNA fragments in the apicomplexans P. falciparum and E. leuckarti (marked in bold in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Six sRNAs are exclusively conserved within cyst-forming Eucoccidians, the closest apicomplexan relatives of T. gondii.
source: Six further sRNAs are exclusively conserved within cyst-forming Eucoccidians, the closest apicomplexan relatives of T. gondii (last column in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Twelve LSU homologs and eleven SSU homologs were found in T. gondii.
source: We could find twelve LSU homologs and eleven SSU homologs in accordance with previous analyses in P. falciparum (Feagin et al., 2012; Hillebrand et al., 2018; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: For the P. falciparum LSU fragment LSUC and the SSU fragment RNA12, no corresponding homologs were identified in T. gondii.
source: Only for the P. falciparum LSU fragment LSUC and the SSU fragment RNA12, we were unable to identify corresponding homologs in T. gondii.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: In most noncoding blocks, the DNA sequence is almost fully used for transcript production.
source: In this and most other noncoding blocks, the DNA sequence is almost fully used for transcript production (see Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in multiple figures.

claim: RNA17, RNA29, and RNA5 were detected at the expected sizes (41 nt, 42 nt, and 83 nt, respectively) by RNA gel blot hybridization.
source: To validate the sequencing data, we performed RNA gel blot hybridization using probes against RNA17, RNA29, and RNA5 (Figure 3B) and indeed detected transcripts of the expected size (41 nt, 42 nt, and 83 nt, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA gel blot hybridization experiment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The transcripts were more abundant in organelle preparations than in input samples, indicating that they are of organellar origin.
source: The transcripts were more abundant in our organelle preparations than in input samples, which indicates that they are of organellar origin and did not originate from NUMTs.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA gel blot hybridization experiment.

claim: 15 transcripts span two blocks.
source: Using block combinations for mapping analysis, we identified 15 transcripts that span two blocks, i.e., there are sRNAs at almost half of all 31 block borders.
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: RNA8 and RNA31 both start in block Fp but end in different blocks.
source: An example of sequences shared at the 5'-end is represented by the pair RNA8 and RNA31, which both start in block Fp but end in different blocks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNA1 and RNA2 both terminate at very similar positions in block Kp but start in different blocks.
source: An example of block sharing at the 3'-end is the RNA pair RNA1/RNA2. Both RNAs terminate at very similar positions in block Kp but start in different blocks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both RNA1 and RNA2 were detected in an RNA gel blot hybridization experiment.
source: Using a probe for the common 3'-part in block Kp, we detected both RNA1 and RNA2 in an RNA gel blot hybridization experiment (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA gel blot hybridization experiment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both RNA1 and RNA2 have homology to E. coli LSU in their 3'-portion via block Kp.
source: Both RNA1 and RNA2 have homology to E. coli LSU in their 3'-portion via block Kp, but only RNA1 has additional homology to E. coli LSU via block I (Figure 4C; Feagin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RNA1 could be used in two positions in the large subunit of the ribosome.
source: It is interesting to consider that RNA1 could, therefore, be used in two positions in the large subunit of the ribosome.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the sequence homology data.

claim: Five RNAs combine sequences from coding and non-protein-coding blocks.
source: In addition to the three pairs of overlapping, noncoding RNAs described above (Figure 4A), we also found five RNAs that combine sequences from coding and non-protein-coding blocks (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: RNA16, RNA23t, and RNA34 were partially antisense to mRNAs.
source: Among them, RNA16, RNA23t, and RNA34 were partially antisense to mRNAs (Figure 5A), and we confirmed the accumulation of RNA34 by RNA gel blot hybridization (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis and RNA gel blot hybridization shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: None of the three antisense RNAs had detectable homologies to E. coli rRNA based on simple sequence searches.
source: None of the three RNAs had detectable homologies to E. coli rRNA based on simple sequence searches, but structural conservation cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: With the exception of RNA34, the RNAs representing a fusion of non-protein-coding regions and protein-coding regions have homologous sequences in the mitochondrial genome of P. falciparum.
source: With the exception of RNA34, the RNAs representing a fusion of non-protein-coding regions and protein-coding regions have homologous sequences in the mitochondrial genome of P. falciparum (Feagin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: In P. falciparum, none of the fusion RNAs are antisense to coding regions.
source: In P. falciparum, however, none of them are antisense to coding regions.
evidence: This is a comparison with P. falciparum based on previous knowledge.

claim: RNA19 contains the coxIII coding sequence adjacent to the cob coding region by a combination of block J and block E.
source: RNA19 contains the coxIII coding sequence adjacent to the cob coding region by a combination of block J and block E (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The 5'-end of the cob mRNA is 6 nt upstream of the second start codon and 10 nt downstream of RNA19.
source: Using rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE), we showed that the 5'-end of the cob mRNA is 6 nt upstream of the second start codon and 10 nt downstream of RNA19 (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is a result from the RACE experiment shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The 3'-end of RNA19 is possibly generated during the formation of the 5'-end of cob.
source: Being only four nucleotides apart, the 3'-end of RNA19 is possibly generated during the formation of the 5'-end of cob.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proximity of the RNA19 3'-end and the cob 5'-end.

claim: RNA19 is conserved in other apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes.
source: RNA19 is conserved in other apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes (Figure 5E) but is not part of open reading frames in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Homologies and a structural fit to the SSU rRNA of E. coli have been noted for P. falciparum RNA19.
source: Homologies and a structural fit to the SSU rRNA of E. coli have been noted for P. falciparum RNA19 (Figure 5E, Feagin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: This sequence similarity to rRNA is maintained in T. gondii.
source: This sequence similarity to rRNA is maintained in T. gondii (Figure 5E), which suggests that despite overlapping with coxIII coding sequence at the J-E block border, RNA19 is functional.
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: RNA3 is situated at the S-R block border.
source: In addition to RNA19, a second RNA-encompassing coding sequence is RNA3, which is situated at the S-R block border (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Block S is part of the coxI coding region - its terminal 22 nucleotides contribute to RNA3.
source: Block S is part of the coxI coding region - its terminal 22 nucleotides contribute to RNA3.
evidence: This is a result from the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The similarity to E. coli 23 S rRNA is restricted to the noncoding block R.
source: The similarity to E. coli 23 S rRNA is, however, restricted to the noncoding block R (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Block S sequence in RNA3 is a 5'-extension of this rRNA.
source: The Block S sequence in RNA3 is, therefore, a 5'-extension of this rRNA, and it remains to be determined whether this is of functional consequence for the mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The presence of a large Megadalton complex containing nuclear-encoded ribosomal proteins targeted to mitochondria has been shown by blue native gel electrophoresis.
source: Additionally, the presence of a large Megadalton complex containing nuclear-encoded ribosomal proteins targeted to mitochondria has been shown by blue native gel electrophoresis (Lacombe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: All tested sRNAs were found to migrate into the deepest gradient fractions 12–14.
source: Second, all tested sRNAs were found to also migrate into the deepest gradient fractions 12–14.
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: The sRNAs are predominantly part of high molecular weight complexes.
source: Collectively, these observations strongly indicate that the sRNAs in question are predominantly part of high molecular weight complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: For all sRNAs examined, a shift was observed from the deeper to the earlier fractions under dissociative conditions.
source: For all sRNAs examined, a shift was observed from the deeper to the earlier fractions under dissociative conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The large molecular weight complexes, with which these sRNAs are associated, are susceptible to ribosome-dissociative conditions.
source: This shift indicates that the large molecular weight complexes, with which these sRNAs are associated, are susceptible to ribosome-dissociative conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: All sRNAs tested are rRNAs.
source: The most parsimonious conclusion is that all sRNAs tested are rRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: rRNAs presumed to be small subunit rRNAs, namely SSUA and RNA 19, displayed signals in fraction 6.
source: We found that rRNAs presumed to be small subunit rRNAs, namely SSUA and RNA 19, displayed signals in fraction 6 (Figure 6D and G), a pattern not observed or less pronounced in presumed LSU rRNAs such as LSUD/E, LSUF/G, RNA1 +2, and RNA3 (Figure 6B, C, E and F).
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The SSU-specific signal in fraction 6 persisted under both standard and dissociative conditions, implying that it represents free SSU.
source: The SSU-specific signal in fraction 6 persisted under both standard and dissociative conditions, implying that it represents free SSU (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The distribution and peaks differ markedly between the four predicted LSU rRNAs and the two SSU sRNAs under dissociative conditions.
source: This shows that under dissociative conditions, the distribution and peaks differ markedly between the four predicted LSU rRNAs and the two SSU sRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA29 likely belongs to the LSU category.
source: This pattern indicates that RNA29 likely belongs to the LSU category.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: RNA29 showed strong signals in the low molecular weight fractions 1–5, hinting at a proportion of unassembled RNA29 in the preparation.
source: Unlike most other rRNAs, RNA29 also showed strong signals in the low molecular weight fractions 1–5 (Figure 6H), hinting at a proportion of unassembled RNA29 in our preparation.
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both RNA1 and RNA2 are assembled into ribosomes.
source: Together this leads to the conclusion that RNA1 and RNA2 are both assembled into ribosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: Despite containing sequences derived from mRNAs, both RNA19 and RNA3 are incorporated into ribosomes.
source: We furthermore observed that despite containing sequences derived from mRNAs, both RNA19 and RNA3 are incorporated into ribosomes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The smaller RNA19 transcripts are observed to migrate into the high-molecular weight fractions, which is EDTA-sensitive.
source: Conversely, the smaller RNA19 transcripts are observed to migrate into the high-molecular weight fractions, which is EDTA-sensitive (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: All three mRNAs migrated deep into the gradient, reaching their peak in fractions 11–13.
source: All three mRNAs migrated deep into the gradient, reaching their peak in fractions 11–13, as depicted in Figure 7B–D.
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: Upon treatment with EDTA, the mRNAs shifted towards fractions associated with lower molecular weights.
source: Upon treatment with EDTA, the mRNAs shifted towards fractions associated with lower molecular weights.
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: Mitochondrial mRNAs in T. gondii are populated with ribosomes.
source: We conclude that mitochondrial mRNAs in T. gondii are populated with ribosomes, which directly supports previous suggestions of active translation in apicomplexan mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: TGRH88_003980_t1 was identified as a potential mitoribosomal protein L11 in previous in silico screens.
source: We chose TGRH88_003980_t1, which was in previous in silico screens identified as a potential mitoribosomal protein L11 (Gupta et al., 2014; Lacombe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: The HA-signal co-localized with the mitochondrial marker protein TgTom40 confirming the localization of TguL11m to T. gondii mitochondria.
source: The HA-signal co-localized with the mitochondrial marker protein TgTom40 (van Dooren et al., 2016) confirming the localization of TguL11m to T. gondii mitochondria (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a result from the immunofluorescence assay shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TguL11m:HA was found with a main peak in fractions 9–11 with signals reaching into the deepest fractions of the gradients.
source: We next analyzed the distribution of TguL11m:HA in sucrose gradients and found a main peak in fractions 9–11 with signals reaching into the deepest fractions of the gradients (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Upon EDTA treatment, the signal shifts from the deepest fractions (12-14) into lower fractions (8-10).
source: Upon EDTA treatment, the signal shifts from the deepest fractions (12-14) into lower fractions (8-10), suggesting that we observe polysomes in fractions 11–14 and that the large subunit of the ribosome is found in fractions 8–10.
evidence: This is a result from the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: The improved sequencing depth revealed strong constraints on the allowed block combinations in T. gondii mtDNA.
source: Thus, a limited number of allowed recombination sites generates the variety of actual DNA fragments sequenced. The question remains whether the constraints outlined in the comprehensive model of mitochondrial genome architecture presented here indicate functional features.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DNA sequencing analysis.

claim: T. gondii appears to be as economical with its mitochondrial sequence space as other apicomplexans, and it does have hardly any unused noncoding sequences in its genome.
source: T. gondii appears to be as economical with its mitochondrial sequence space as other apicomplexans, and it does have hardly any unused noncoding sequences in its genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the small RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Both strands of apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes are transcribed in full.
source: Similar antisense degradation mechanisms must be assumed in apicomplexans, as both strands of their genomes are transcribed in full (Rehkopf et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: Sequences homologous to rRNAs have been found in many coding regions in sense and antisense orientation.
source: Sequences homologous to rRNAs have been found in many coding regions in sense and antisense orientation (Mauro and Edelman, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: It has been suggested that this could link ribosome production to other cellular processes by reciprocal inhibition of mRNA and rRNA expression.
source: It has been suggested that this could link ribosome production to other cellular processes by reciprocal inhibition of mRNA and rRNA expression (Coelho et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation to support it.

claim: Using blue-native gel electrophoresis, it was demonstrated that tagged ribosomal proteins TgmS35, TgbL12m, TguL3m, and TguL24m migrate as constituents of a macromolecular complex within the size range of a ribosome.
source: Using blue-native gel electrophoresis, it was demonstrated that tagged ribosomal proteins TgmS35, TgbL12m, TguL3m, and TguL24m migrate as constituents of a macromolecular complex within the size range of a ribosome (Lacombe et al., 2019; Shikha et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: TgmS35 and TguL24m coprecipitated with mitochondria-encoded rRNA.
source: Additionally, TgmS35 and TguL24m coprecipitated with mitochondria-encoded rRNA.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on previous studies.

claim: Knockdown of TgmS35, TgbL35m, TgbL36m, and TgbL28m resulted in a specific loss of activity of one respiratory complex, which is partially encoded in the mitochondrial genome.
source: Knockdown of TgmS35, TgbL35m, TgbL36m, and TgbL28m resulted in a specific loss of activity of one respiratory complex, which is partially encoded in the mitochondrial genome (Lacombe et al., 2019; Shikha et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: The study provides evidence that sRNAs with homology to rRNA are part of polysomes.
source: Here, we provide evidence that sRNAs with homology to rRNA are part of polysomes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings strongly support the notion of active translation by mitochondrial ribosomes in tachyzoites of T. gondii.
source: In sum, our findings strongly support the notion of active translation by mitochondrial ribosomes in tachyzoites of T. gondii, and demonstrate that most if not all mitochondrial small RNAs fragments are part of the apicomplexan mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Most if not all mitochondrial small RNAs fragments are part of the apicomplexan mitochondrial ribosome.
source: In sum, our findings strongly support the notion of active translation by mitochondrial ribosomes in tachyzoites of T. gondii, and demonstrate that most if not all mitochondrial small RNAs fragments are part of the apicomplexan mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: RNA2 and RNA29 might not integrate into ribosomes as effectively as other rRNA fragments.
source: This suggests that RNA2 and RNA29 might not integrate into ribosomes as effectively as other rRNA fragments, raising questions about the coordination of rRNA fragment assembly.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the sucrose gradient analysis.

claim: In the case of RNA19, processing precedes integration.
source: Notably, longer variants of RNA19 are not incorporated into ribosomes, unlike smaller isoforms, highlighting a connection between small RNA processing and ribosome assembly. In the case of RNA19, processing precedes integration, contrasting with plant chloroplast ribosomes where the 23 S rRNA is split endonucleolytically at two sites post-integration (Liu et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sucrose gradient analysis and comparison with plant chloroplast ribosomes.

claim: In plant chloroplast ribosomes, the 23 S rRNA is split endonucleolytically at two sites post-integration.
source: In the case of RNA19, processing precedes integration, contrasting with plant chloroplast ribosomes where the 23 S rRNA is split endonucleolytically at two sites post-integration (Liu et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations to support it.

claim: Apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes are vital for organism survival, expressing key respiratory chain and gene expression components, particularly ribosomes.
source: Apicomplexan mitochondrial genomes are vital for organism survival, expressing key respiratory chain and gene expression components, particularly ribosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions section.

claim: Most if not all mitochondrial sRNAs are components of active ribosomes that assemble into polysomes.
source: We conclude that most if not all mitochondrial sRNAs are components of active ribosomes that assemble into polysomes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: T. gondii's dynamic block-based genome organization leads to the usage of mitochondrial sequences in mRNA as well as rRNA contexts.
source: T. gondii's dynamic block-based genome organization leads to the usage of mitochondrial sequences in mRNA as well as rRNA contexts, potentially linking rRNA and mRNA expression regulation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.
